claims.claim: The load is mostly waiting on sockets, and Node's event loop handles this well
claims.measured: I/O wait test (10 ms per request, 256 connections): node-express 14,188 req/s, p99 35.39 ms; node-fastify 17,462 req/s, p99 27.96 ms; for comparison go-gin 20,235 and go-nethttp 18,905
claims.why: In the I/O wait test Node serves 14–17k req/s on one core, within 1.5x of Go and the other fast runtimes, so it handles I/O-bound waiting well.

claims.claim: A few small Fly machines will cover about 2,500 outbound deliveries/s with 2,500–5,000 requests in flight at 0.3–2 s each
claims.why: The benchmarks measure inbound server throughput with 10 ms waits and at most 256 connections, not thousands of long-lived outbound client connections.

claims.claim: Go would use less memory per connection than Node
claims.measured: I/O wait, 256 connections: go-gin 16 MB, go-nethttp 15 MB vs node-express 68 MB, node-fastify 69 MB peak memory
claims.why: Go used about 4x less memory than Node holding the same 256 concurrent connections, so the direction is right.

claims.claim: Go would use less CPU for TLS than Node
claims.why: None of the tests use TLS. In the plain-HTTP I/O wait test, Go used less CPU (47–57%) than Node (76–92%) at similar or higher throughput.

claims.claim: Go's performance gain over Node is marginal at this scale and might save tens of dollars a month
claims.measured: I/O wait: go-gin 20,235 req/s vs node-fastify 17,462 / node-express 14,188 req/s
claims.why: The measurements show Go about 1.2–1.4x ahead on I/O-bound work but give no cloud cost figures, so the dollar estimate can't be checked.

claims.claim: Node's DNS lookup uses the libuv thread pool (default 4 threads), so slow customer DNS can stall every delivery
claims.why: The benchmarks don't measure DNS resolution or thread-pool behaviour.
